title: ProtocolMatch: Protocol-Dependent Model Selection for Scientific Dynamics Forecasting
authors: Lu Wei, Yufeng Wang, Haibin Ling
abstract: Scientific dynamics forecasting is often framed as an architecture choice, although deployment is also determined by observed history, rollout feedback, compute budget, physical objective, and test distribution. We formulate protocol-dependent model selection and introduce ProtocolMatch, a compute-matched, validation-selected, and failure-preserving evaluation framework. On driven quantum-spin dynamics, we compare recurrent, patched-attention, causal-attention, and low-rank linear predictors across three independently generated datasets. The causal-attention--recurrence ordering reverses as the training set grows within a fixed two-spin task, while a linear predictor has the lowest mean error in the six-spin local-observable comparison. Restricting observed history worsens every refreshed-history view but improves every closed-loop view in the four-spin study. A latest-state MLP has lower error than persistence on every dataset under state refresh across all five cells, yet its closed-loop rank varies by system and includes finite explosive errors. Physical penalties improve targeted consistency without reliably improving prediction error, and in-distribution intervals lose most coverage after a driving-frequency shift. Thus scientific model selection should return a predictor with its protocol and report accuracy, physical validity, and shifted-distribution reliability separately.
summary: This paper addresses the challenge of model selection in quantum dynamics forecasting by proposing ProtocolMatch, a framework that evaluates models based on the entire operational protocol, not just the architecture. By testing on driven quantum-spin systems, the authors show that model performance is highly protocol-dependent, necessitating that any reported predictor must be accompanied by its specific operational context and separate reliability metrics.
main_problem: Scientific dynamics forecasting requires model selection that accounts for the entire 'protocol'—including observation history, rollout rules, and physical constraints—rather than just the model architecture.
main_result: The optimal forecasting model depends critically on the specific protocol used, as demonstrated by performance reversals when changing data size, history length, or evaluation loop (observed vs. closed-loop).
method: The authors introduce ProtocolMatch, a framework that evaluates model candidates by explicitly conditioning the risk calculation on the entire forecasting protocol $P$, separating accuracy, physical validity, and shifted-distribution reliability.
model_or_system: The study applies this framework to driven quantum-spin dynamics, simulating systems ranging from two-spin to six-spin quantum chains governed by Hamiltonians like the transverse-field Ising model.
key_observables: Mean Squared Error (MSE) for prediction error, physical consistency (e.g., trace normalization, positivity), and interval coverage under shifted distributions.
important_parameters: History length (1, 5, 20), rollout rule (Observed-history vs. Closed-loop), and the specific protocol tuple $P$ defining the evaluation regime.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the protocol cannot be treated as a nuisance variable; changes in performance across protocols indicate fundamentally different deployment behaviors.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison between observed-history and closed-loop evaluations, and show how the preferred model architecture reverses when varying training data size or rollout rules.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitations of architecture-only model selection, introduces the ProtocolMatch framework to condition model selection on the full protocol $P$, and then empirically tests this framework across various quantum-spin dynamics systems and protocols.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, machine-learning-informed methodology for assessing the reliability of quantum dynamics models, which is crucial for building trustworthy simulations of open quantum systems.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: The forecasting protocol determines both the information available to a predictor and how that predictor is compared. (a) Observed-history and closed-loop evaluation keep the predictor, future controls, and target fixed; only the source of the next state-history window changes. (b) ProtocolMatch pairs that declared task with controlled candidates, validation-only selection, independent-dataset aggregation, and failure-preserving reliability reports.
Figure 1(b) summarizes the comparison workflow. Four controls make the resulting rank interpretable.

Figure 2: Replicated ranking reversals under matched optimization time. (a) LSTM-minus-causal error for closed-loop extrapolation changes sign between 64 and 256 training trajectories. (b) Local-minus-full-history error changes sign between observed-history and closed-loop rollout while the full prediction target remains fixed. Colored lines are independent-dataset means over three training seeds; the dashed black line is their average. Both panels use 20-step histories, a 120-second budget, identity-distribution tests, and no output clipping.

Figure 2(b) defines the input contrast as local-minus- full MSE. For the history-20 LSTM, it is +0.02046 with observed-history refresh and −0.03023 with closed-loop feedback. Each independent dataset shows the same sign change. The benefit of nonlocal history therefore depends on whether those channels are refreshed from observations or populated by preceding predictions.

Figure 3: Accuracy, physical validity, and uncertainty are distinct outcomes. (a) A trace penalty usually lowers trace error but often raises prediction MSE for a two-spin LSTM; the 32 correlated views share fitted models. (b) Intervals calibrated on 64 independent identity-distribution trajectories approach nominal 90% coverage in distribution but lose most coverage after a frequency shift. Widths are full symmetric interval widths.
